newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Inter-Korean Red Cross talks to resume in Beijing.
newsitem.headline: Inter-Korean Red Cross talks to resume in Beijing.

text.p: Inter-Korean Red Cross talks on speeding up food aid to the hungry North will resume on Friday in Beijing after the South Korean side backed down and agreed on the Chinese capital as a venue.
The Southern Red Cross reluctantly agreed to Beijing in a message to the North on Tuesday sent over a telephone "hotline" at the border village of Panmunjom, a statement said.
An earlier round of talks on May 3 and 5 -- the first between the two sides for almost five years -- were also held in Beijing.

But they broke down after the hunger-sticken North demanded to know the exact amount of aid it could expect before discussing moves to speed delivery. The South has since agreed to reveal the size of donations.
The South Korean Red Cross has proposed sending food directly to the North, instead of through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
It also wants to deliver aid through the land border at Panmunjom to cut transport costs. Aid is now sent by ship or by train through China.

The issue of the venue of discussions, and direct shipments, have a political as well as practical importance. South Korean officials have said they hoped Red Cross contacts would develop into wider cross-border exchanges.
But Pyongyang is anxious to avoid direct dealings at any level with the South. The two Koreas are still technically at war after their 1950-53 conflict ended only in a truce.

"I have decided to send delegates to Beijing with a view to solving the difficulties our brethren in North Korea are suffering as quickly as possible," the president of the South Korean Red Cross, Kang Young-hoon, said in the "hotline" message.
"I still do not understand the real intention behind your insistence on holding the meeting in Beijing, rather than in our country, which would be more convenient. It is regrettable," he said.
The Southern side had proposed a gathering in either Seoul, Pyongyang or Panmunjom.
On Saturday, the South Korean Red Cross said the Northern side was now demanding to know what kind of food aid would be sent, and the timing of the aid.

The South is due to deliver 3,600 tonnes of Chinese corn by train next week from China, the first batch of 15,000 tonnes donated by Southern civic groups to help stave off famine in the impoverished Stalinist nation.
The Red Cross is the only legal channel for private aid from South Korea to the North.
Last Friday, the South Korean government pledged fresh food aid worth $10 million to a U.N. appeal for North Korea.

The promise of 50,000 tonnes of corn and 300 tonnes of powdered milk is on top of $6 million already delivered to the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP), which has appealed for 200,000 tonnes of aid worth $98.5 million.
The United States has pledged $25 million to the WFP.

Pyongyang has demanded massive food aid as a condition for joining proposed peace talks with the South, the United States and China. Seoul and Washington have said large-scale aid can only be discussed at peace talks.
